title: Number Line Hopscotch
strapline: Count with your whole body — numbers you jump along instead of just point at.
intent: Children build a secure sense of the counting order by moving through it — one square, one jump, one number word.
Children connect numerals to quantities and to position: 5 is a symbol, a place on the line, and five jumps away.
Children explore adding and taking away as movement — hop forward two, jump back one — long before it's written down.
Children develop gross-motor control, balance and rhythm while the maths hides inside the game.
Children turn number into something social and joyful, chanting and cheering each other along the line.
implementation: Chalk or tape a big number line 0–10 on the ground outdoors, numerals large and bold, one number per square.
Model it first: hop and say each number aloud, landing squarely — 'one, two, THREE' — so the count and the jump match.
Pose whole-body problems: 'start on 3, jump forward 2 — where did you land?' and let them discover 5.
Add a big foam dice or spinner so the number of jumps is decided by chance, and children read it to move.
Feed in the language of position and change — before, after, forward, back, one more, one less — as they play.
Let confident children run the game: calling numbers, setting challenges, checking each other's landings.
Take it inside on rainy days with a taped line along the carpet, or shrink it to a tabletop track with a counter.
key_questions: If you jump forward two from three, where will you land — shall we check?
Which number comes just before this one?
How many jumps to get all the way to ten?
What number is one more than the one you're on?
Can you land on every number without missing one?

impact.text: Children say number names in order and match one jump to one number.
Children recognise numerals and find their place along the line.
Children solve 'one more' and 'one less' problems by moving along the line.
Children use positional language — forward, back, before, after — as they play.
Children hop, balance and land with growing coordination and control.
Children take turns, cheer each other on and set their own challenges.

enhancements: A giant foam dice or a spinner to decide how many jumps to take.
Number pebbles or beanbags to toss and then hop to.
A 0–20 line for children ready to count beyond ten.
A washing-line version at head height with pegged numeral cards that go missing overnight.
Chalk arrows and '+2 / -1' cards to turn hops into simple sums.
A frog or bunny puppet who can only reach the flower by making the right number of jumps.

playing_exploring: Children invent their own rules, routes and challenges along the line.
The count becomes a game they choose to play again and again.
active_learning: Children keep going to reach ten, retrying when they miss a number.
Landing on exactly the right number delivers a win they chase again.
creating_thinking: Children predict where a jump will land, then test it with their feet.
They spot the pattern of the counting order and use it to plan their moves.
